subjects.label: Counter-revolution: origins, definition, and historical scope
subjects.meaning: The emergence of a counter-revolutionary outlook after the claim of national sovereignty in June 1789, and the chapter's distinction between armed restoration, anti-revolutionary resistance, and later constitutional royalism.
subjects.stance: Counter-revolution began as a reaction to the new regime rather than as a pre-existing unified doctrine; the author narrows the term and rejects indiscriminate revolutionary labeling of all resistance.

evidence.evidence_summary: Defines counter-revolution as a response formed only after the June 1789 assertion of national sovereignty and identifies the Royal Session as its first serious act.
Distinguishes armed overthrow from local resistance and argues that authorities too readily labeled opposition counter-revolutionary.
Contrasts failed armed restoration with the surviving possibility of constitutional monarchy through elections.

subjects.label: Émigré counter-revolution: organization, army, and collapse
subjects.meaning: Successive émigré waves built courts, committees, and an auxiliary army, retaining old hierarchies while accepting real personal sacrifices. Varennes accelerated officer emigration and militarization; the collapse after Valmy dispersed the main princely forces, leaving foreign-dependent remnants.
subjects.stance: Neither a uniform aristocratic exodus nor an autonomous restoration army: sincere loyalty coexisted with status rivalry, logistical weakness, unrealistic expectations, and dependence on foreign strategy. The retreat after Valmy, rather than émigré participation in its cannonade, shattered the armed project.

evidence.evidence_summary: Traces the first emigration after July 1789, frontier committees, and Artois's Turin organization.
Institutional abolition, army unrest, and church policy drew nobles, officers, magistrates, and clergy into emigration.
Varennes accelerated officer departures and transformed émigré rescue ambitions.
Former officers formed an army centred on Koblenz, intended as an auxiliary to foreign armies.
Exile courts reproduced precedence disputes and suspicion of latecomers; the portrait is qualified by recognition of sacrifice.
Loyalty and risk qualified the portrait of selfish exile; subsidies, supply failure, disbandment, and refusal of amnesty reveal practical weakness.
The retreat after Valmy shattered princely formations; Condé alone retained a corps in imperial service and émigrés dispersed.
Concludes that feuding émigrés had no independent chance of arresting, moderating, or reversing events in France.

subjects.label: Counter-revolutionary factionalism
subjects.meaning: Persistent divisions among early 'pure' émigrés, constitutional monarchists, royal agents, popular rebels, and competing leaders.
subjects.stance: Counter-revolution was never unified; mutual suspicion and ideological rivalry repeatedly obstructed cooperation and outlasted military defeat.

evidence.evidence_summary: States at the outset that counter-revolution was no more a unity than the Revolution it opposed.
Contrasts 'pures' committed to pre-1789 restoration with diverse constitutional monarchists who accepted a representative constitution.
Shows post-Quiberon recrimination, conspiracy claims, and conflict over Puisaye's leadership.
Attributes counter-revolutionary failure in part to vicious feuding among groups that mistrusted one another.

subjects.label: Restoration programmes and the constitutional-monarchist alternative
subjects.meaning: The princes claimed inherited royal authority against the Constitution of 1791 and repeatedly promised restoration of the old institutions and property. Constitutional royalists accepted written representative government; after armed restoration failed, limited monarchy remained an electoral possibility.
subjects.stance: Full restoration and constitutional royalism are different programmes. Their appeal was unequal: the source rejects the viability of old-regime nostalgia while treating limited monarchy as a possible route to stability, not an inevitable outcome.

evidence.evidence_summary: The princes denied the Assembly’s authority and treated royal assent to the constitution as coerced.
Interprets the princes' 1791 manifesto as seeking a free legislative king and an effectively complete restoration of the old regime.
The 1793 regency proclamation promises restoration of Church, orders, old judicial system, and confiscated property.
Sets out constitutional émigré variants united in refusing to return France to the era before written representative government.
Verona deliberately alienated constitutional émigrés and potential right-wing allies.
Argues that nostalgic restoration lacked mass appeal but limited constitutional monarchy could still attract support.

subjects.label: Religion and counter-revolution
subjects.meaning: The Civil Constitution, clerical oath, papal condemnation, and repression of refractories transformed religious allegiance and local resistance into organized opposition. Lay pressure mattered as well as clerical initiative; toleration later weakened insurgent support.
subjects.stance: Religious resistance was neither uniformly manipulated by clergy nor automatically royalist. Treating refractory priests as counter-revolutionaries helped make them so; restoration of worship removed a central grievance.

evidence.evidence_summary: Explains how the clerical oath and papal condemnation turned religious schism into official opposition to the Revolution.
Brittany’s unusually extensive oath refusal and lay support made it promising for La Rouërie’s association.
Connects mass oath refusal, parishioner pressure, deportation policies, and allegiance to Church and king in the west.
Shows that restoration of open worship in 1795 removed a persistent grievance sustaining western insurgents.

subjects.label: Vendée insurgency
subjects.meaning: The Vendéan uprising combined limited material gains, higher rents and taxes, intrusive local government and religious conflict, with conscription as the final trigger. Rebels formed a Catholic and Royal Army, sought British aid, suffered military destruction and reprisals, then renewed fighting before Hoche’s pacification.
subjects.stance: An authentically popular royalist movement with local defensive aims, not an émigré instrument or a proven plan to conquer Paris. Conscription alone does not explain it; republican brutality probably prolonged resistance after destruction of the field army.

evidence.evidence_summary: The March levy activated accumulated grievances among western peasants who had gained comparatively little from the abolition of old burdens.
Higher rents and exactions, religious coercion, and administrative intrusion preceded conscription, which turned resistance into open Catholic and royal identification.
Traces the march to Granville, military destruction at Le Mans and Savenay, and expectations of British aid.
Describes Charette's renewed revolt and the failed attempt to link a British-backed expedition with the Vendée.
Attributes pacification to reinforced counter-insurgency, executions of leaders, toleration, and discipline of republican troops.
Concludes that reprisals prolonged resistance and that the Vendéans were unlikely to project power toward Paris.

subjects.label: Chouannerie in Brittany
subjects.meaning: The decentralized Catholic and royal guerrilla movement in Brittany, its local strength, weak coordination, British contacts, and eventual suppression.
subjects.stance: A locally rooted Catholic and royal guerrilla movement, distinct from the Vendéan field army. Local religious, fiscal, administrative, and conscription grievances sustained it, but scattered bands could not be treated as Puisaye’s unified national army or assumed capable of capturing a port.

evidence.evidence_summary: Western religious and local grievances culminated in open royalism; Breton bands remained guerrillas rather than coalescing as in the Vendée.
Assesses the movement as under 22,000, decentralized and disruptive, but unable to capture and hold a port.
Notes counter-insurgency pressure, defections, supply shortages, and incomplete adherence to La Mabilais.
Shows troop saturation reducing chouan mobility and Puisaye to hiding by 1796.

uncertainties.issue: The source explicitly warns that dissatisfaction and resistance were not automatically restorationist counter-revolution.
uncertainties.handling: Subjects and evidence preserve the author's distinctions; anti-revolutionary episodes are included only where the text establishes royalist, clerical, or organized counter-revolutionary content.

uncertainties.topic: Chapter date in title versus concluding chronology
uncertainties.issue: The chapter title ends at 1795, but the narrative and explicit conclusion carry military defeat and pacification through April 1797.
uncertainties.handling: Retain 1796-1797 evidence because it appears on owned pages and supplies the chapter's conclusion; do not silently force evidence into the title's date range.

uncertainties.issue: Royalists participated in Federalist episodes, but the author denies that the revolt as a whole was counter-revolutionary.
uncertainties.handling: Create a major distinction subject with stance-sensitive access; avoid a heading that equates Federalism with royalism.

uncertainties.issue: His operational advice resembled émigré schemes, but the source explicitly says he was not a counter-revolutionary.
uncertainties.handling: Retain only an optional, qualified subject under constitutional monarchy and royal counsel; prohibit unqualified counter-revolutionary access.

uncertainties.issue: Several named people receive brief illustrative or logistical mentions without independent thematic development.
uncertainties.handling: Do not use density as a quota; retain representative marginal cases as exclude_by_default and record the rest in exclusions rather than silently treating every name as a subject.

uncertainties.issue: Royalist representations and the author’s estimates diverge.
